background.definition: A solitary renal cyst is a fluid filled lesion located within the renal parenchyma. Most cysts are benign and asymptomatic.

list.listitem: Incidence has increased as a result of increasing use of imaging modalities.
Male to female ratio of 2:1; 146 in 1000 males, 77 in 1000 females.
4.7% in the 3rd decade of life, 34.6% in the 7th decade of life.
They are acquired lesions of the kidney, which originate from diverticula of the distal convoluted or collecting tubules.
They are believed to occur as a result of weakening of the tubular basement membrane.
These diverticula increase in number as the kidney ages, which explains an increase in prevalence of cysts with advancing age.
Renal cysts can be found in the outer cortex or in the medulla. They are lined by a flat epithelium and contain fluid that is derived from their parent nephron and/or is secreted by the lining cells.
Cysts may rarely compress surrounding renal parenchyma causing hypertension and/or obstruction of the pelvicaliceal system.
Ultrasound showing a simple or minimally complex renal cyst requires no further evaluation. A

Further imaging (CT or MRI) is recommended for all other cysts, to help categorize them using the Bosniak classification system and to guide subsequent treatment (see ). B A proposed update to the classification aims to improve the original classification’s ability to predict the likelihood of malignancy in renal masses with cystic components. C
Percutaneous biopsy in an indeterminate cystic mass is not recommended. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Multiple unilateral or bilateral renal cysts, positive family history, gross hematuria, flank pain
Multiple unilateral renal cysts on ultrasound or CT of various sizes separated by normal or atrophic parenchyma
Cyst with thickened irregular walls or septa, cyst enhancement on imaging studies
Systemic symptoms, acute onset, imaging studies diagnostic

list.listitem: Vast majority are asymptomatic.
Usually discovered as an incidental finding on an ultrasound, CT or MRI.
May occasionally present with flank pain, hematuria, signs of infection, hypertension or obstruction of the pelvicaliceal system.

If ultrasound shows a simple cyst (no septa) or a minimally complex cyst (up to 2 hairline septa) then no further imaging study is needed. If the cyst is neither a simple nor a minimally complex cyst then it should be further imaged with a CT or MRI. American College of Radiology guidelines state that CT with and without contrast and MRI with and without contrast are equally good options for further evaluation of a nonsimple cyst.
Contrast enhanced ultrasound: contrast-enhanced second-harmonic ultrasound (if available) is appropriate for renal cyst classification using the Bosniak system.
CT with and without contrast: the presence of either nodular or septal enhancement has the highest sensitivity for predicting malignancy.

MRI with and without contrast: the presence of solid enhancing nodular components with high resolution 3D MRI provides excellent positive predictive value for diagnosing neoplastic cystic renal lesions. There is a 95% likelihood that cystic renal lesions with focal nodular enhancement are malignant. MRI is useful for characterizing a complex cystic renal mass because lesion enhancement can be evaluated. MRI has a better contrast resolution compared to CT, sometimes there will be findings on MRI (specifically the T2 weighted images) that cannot be identified on the correlative CT images.
Percutaneous biopsy in an indeterminate cystic mass is unreliable, hence not recommended (a negative biopsy cannot rule out the absence of malignancy).
If ultrasound shows a simple cyst (no septa) or a minimally complex cyst (up to 2 hairline septa) then no further imaging is needed. All other cysts should be imaged with a CT or MRI (see ).
Based on CT/MRI results, the cyst is categorized by the Bosniak classification (), which guides subsequent therapy.
Asymptomatic solitary renal cysts (Bosniak I, II) require no further management. A
Treatment of choice for symptomatic renal cysts (Bosniak I, II) is percutaneous aspiration with injection of sclerosant. Sodium tetradecyl sulfate (STDS) is preferred since it causes less pain. B
Calcium channel blockers are not preferred in treatment of hypertension in patients with renal cysts due to a possible increase in cyst size. C
Any Bosniak category III or IV cyst requires surgical removal. Surgical treatment of choice is retroperitoneal laparoscopic decortication. B
No specific medical therapy is available. For pain associated with the cyst consider NSAIDs or acetaminophen.
For cyst infection consider antibiotic therapy.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and diuretics are favored over calcium channel blockers in hypertensives due to the possibility of cyst enlargement with calcium channel blockers.
If symptoms are not controlled with the medications mentioned above, one of the following options can be discussed with the patient with a Bosniak I or II category cyst.
Percutaneous aspiration without injection of sclerosant has a high recurrence rate.

Percutaneous cyst aspiration with injection of a sclerosant (eg, ethanol, STDS) has a complete ablation rate of 82% with ethanol and 76% with STDS, partial regression rate of 9% with ethanol and 18% with STDS, with failure of resolution in the remainder. STDS is preferred as first choice since patients report less pain.

A systematic review identified 57 studies with 4071 patients (mostly observational) and found that 88% of patients undergoing aspiration with sclerotherapy had a treatment success defined as >50% reduction in cyst size and resolutiono f symptoms. Only 0.1% had major complications, while 11% had minor, transient complications.

Retroperitoneal laparoscopic decortication has an ablation rate of 100%, with immediate postoperative symptomatic relief, a short convalescence period and a favorable 5-year clinical outcome. Recommended for patients with symptomatic cysts that are Bosniak category I or II. A systematic review of case series and randomized trials found that for 596 patients undergoing laparoscopic decortication, complete radiologic resolution occurred in 96%, 95% were symptom free, less than 1% had intraoperative complications, and 1.4% had post-operative complications.

Open surgical cyst decortication has an ablation rate of 100% but significant perioperative and postoperative morbidity and prolonged hospital stay. It may be considered for patients with symptomatic cysts that are Bosniak category I or II.
Partial nephrectomy is recommended for cysts that are Bosniak III or IV.
If symptomatic treatment with medications does not provide sufficient relief refer to a nephrologist, urologist, or surgeon.
If Bosniak III or IV refer to urologist or surgeon for further evaluation.
Simple renal cysts increase in size at a rate of 1.6 mm per year. Renal cysts tend to increase more rapidly in younger patients, and stabilize or show less growth with advancing age. B
The risk of malignancy in a simple renal cyst is 0.12%. B
Patients with a large cyst or a peripherally located cyst can be at a higher risk for developing hypertension. B
There are only case reports of hemorrhage within a renal cyst. C
Follow-up Bosniak category IIF cyst with a CT scan in 6 months following the first CT and then yearly for up to 5 years. Younger patients may need longer follow-up. C
A watchful waiting approach may be appropriate for elderly persons with Bosniak class III lesions, especially those with high surgical risk.
Nephrectomy (partial) may be appropriate in young patients with a Bosniak category IIF lesion to alleviate patient and parental anxiety.

cell.label: Simple cyst (no septa) or minimally complex cyst (1 or 2 hairline thin septa) on initial imaging (usually ultrasound)?
NSAIDs or acetaminophen for pain; consider aspiration with or without sclerosants, or surgical decortication (open or laparoscopic).

feature.caption: Bosniak Classification of Solitary Renal Cyst and Recommended Management.

tr.td: Benign simple cyst, hairline thin wall, no septa, calcifications or solid components, water density, no enhancement
No follow-up needed. Consider treatment (aspiration with or without sclerosant) if symptomatic
Benign simple cyst, may contain few hairline thin septa, fine calcification or short segment of slightly thickened calcification, may enhance; uniformly high attenuation nonenhancing lesions <3 cm
No follow-up needed. Consider treatment (aspiration with or without sclerosant) if symptomatic
Multiple hairline thin septa or minimal smooth thickening of wall/septa, well marginated and uniformly high attenuation nonenhancing lesions <3 cm
"Indeterminate" cystic lesions: thickened irregular or smooth walls/septa, enhancement. Examples include hemorrhagic cysts, chronic infected cysts, and cystic renal cell carcinoma
May be benign or malignant; requires surgery
Thickened irregular or smooth walls/septa, enhancement, also containing enhancing adjacent soft-tissue components. Includes clearly malignant lesions (eg, cystic renal cell carcinoma)
